caption: $53bn returned to shareholders 2004-2013: $27.8bn of dividends and $25.4bn of share buybacks. No share repurchase has been made since 2012.
The 2014 bridge to the '>$45bn by 2023' ambition: established products roll off, growth platforms sustain 2013-2017, then the late-stage pipeline takes over to 2023.

The 2014 capital-allocation framework, before buybacks disappeared from it: cash flow to R&D and business development, progressive dividend, efficient capital structure, against 14 Phase III / 26 Phase II / 39 Phase I NMEs.
The 2014 late-stage bet as it was placed: every NME plotted on potential peak-year sales against strength of evidence, including AZD9291 (Tagrisso), MEDI4736 (Imfinzi), Lynparza and benralizumab.

The only quantified R&D-productivity disclosure anywhere in the deck archive: cost per candidate drug $50-60m against an $80-110m industry benchmark, and probability of success up from about 6% to about 16% since 2010.
China before volume-based procurement: number-two multinational, largest MNC sales force, 9M 2014 sales of $1.7bn growing 22% at CER, field force of 5,694.

Alexion as underwritten in December 2020: 20% revenue CAGR 2017 to 2020 LTM, 11 molecules in more than 20 studies, Ultomiris exclusivity to 2035, and about 70% of PNH patients switched off Soliris within 18 months.
Pro-forma combined company at announcement: $32bn Total Revenue growing 10%, 32% Core operating profit margin, $11bn EBITDA and $28bn net debt including about $13.5bn of acquisition debt.
Alexion deal terms: $175 per share, $39.4bn total consideration split $13.5bn cash and $25.9bn stock, with Alexion holders taking about 15% of the combined company.

The entire loss-of-exclusivity wave, disclosed five years early. US patent expiry for 19 products, from Brilinta around 2024 and Farxiga around 2025 through Tagrisso and Calquence around 2031 to Ultomiris in 2035.
The Alexion consolidation boundary: standalone H1 2021 revenue by medicine, Soliris $2,099m, Ultomiris $1,071m, Strensiq $405m, immediately before AstraZeneca began reporting Rare Disease.
AI applied to operations, quantified: 50% less synthetic route-design lead time, over 20% higher manufacturing yield, and 90% less dispensing planning time.
The ambition that was superseded ten months later: low-double-digit Total Revenue CAGR 2021-2025 off a pro-forma 2021 base, and at least 15 NMEs approved by 2030.
Total Revenue ex-COVID 2012-2023: $28.0bn down to a $22.1bn trough in 2018, then up to $45.8bn in 2023. This is the slide management uses to claim it delivered the 2014 ambition.

The $80bn-by-2030 bridge: loss of exclusivity (Brilinta, Farxiga, Lynparza, Soliris) and IRA impact as named negative bars, 13 existing medicines and 15 launching NMEs as the offset. Marked illustrative, not to scale.
Emerging Markets at 29% of Total Revenue, with China growth decelerating from 41% in 2021 to 4%, then -1% and 8%. The warning was visible two years before the 2026 decline.
Rare Disease patient growth of 18%, 21% and 25% against revenue growth of 10%, 12% and 16%. Revenue per patient is falling roughly 7% a year as Soliris converts to Ultomiris and geography broadens.
Lung-cancer franchise US market shares: FLAURA 73%, PACIFIC 67%, ADAURA 67%, alongside the diagnostic and treatment-rate expansion AstraZeneca funded to create the market.

ADC target coverage of 78-100% across seven tumour types, against future G7 ADC-treated patient pools from 310k in NSCLC down to 40k in endometrial cancer, and a stated vision of 2-3 foundational ADCs per major tumour.
Cash conversion 2020-2023: operating cash flow $4.8bn to $10.3bn, and 18% to 22.5% of Total Revenue with a Vaxzevria-depressed 16% in 2021.

Capital allocation with no buyback line: reinvestment, progressive dividend, investment-grade rating, business development. Dividend increments of $0.10 in 2022 and $0.20 in 2024, at 1.9x net debt to adjusted EBITDA.
The mid-30s% Core operating margin target for 2026, a number that appears nowhere in the filings, and the SG&A levers behind it, which include loss of exclusivity enabling resource redeployment.
Pipeline value density: 81, 77, 84 then 91 late-stage trials from FY2021 to FY2024, with average non-risk-adjusted peak-year revenue per trial passing $1bn.

The distribution-leverage case for baxdrostat: over 20m US and over 75m ex-US uncontrolled 2L+ hypertension patients, about 85% managed in primary care, and over 90% of cardiologists already reached by the existing CVRM footprint.

The ADC platform map colour-coded by ownership: Enhertu and Datroway as alliance ADCs against seven wholly-owned and five proprietary-platform ADCs. The mix shift moves ADC revenue from alliance gross-profit share to full Product Sales.

Unique Phase III and registration assets rising from 27 to 37 between 2021 and 2025, while average non-risk-adjusted peak-year revenue per indication roughly doubles to about $1.3bn. Trial patients 57k then 61k.

The US repositioning on one slide: $5bn of new Virginia and Texas capacity, 131 US manufacturing sites, a NYSE direct listing approved by 99.36% of the shareholder vote, and a government agreement trading Medicaid MFN pricing for a three-year tariff exemption plus direct-to-consumer sales.

Where the operating leverage comes from: Core R&D rising to about 23.5% of Total Revenue while Core SG&A falls to about 26%. The mid-30%s Core operating margin target is footnoted as struck at Q1 2024 exchange rates.
Per-asset non-risk-adjusted peak-year revenue guidance in $5bn-plus and $3-5bn buckets, a forecast layer that appears zero times in the annual report.
The current state at H1 2026: Oncology $14.1bn up 15% and now 46% of Product Revenue, CVRM $6.0bn down 12% on the Farxiga loss of exclusivity, China $3.5bn down 5% on volume-based procurement.
The 2026 P&L modelling table line by line: gross margin stable to slightly better, Core R&D at the upper end of the low-20%s, and Core finance expenses the one line guided higher than 2025.
